summary: This proposed standard specifies a registration mechanism for the Host Identity Protocol, letting hosts register with services such as rendezvous servers or middleboxes. It obsoletes RFC 5203.

plainLanguage.summary:
The Host Identity Protocol lets a host prove who it is without using its IP address. Some hosts also need a service: a rendezvous server to help them find other hosts, or a middlebox that lets their packets through a firewall.

This RFC is the sign-up procedure. The service provider says in the handshake which services it has and how long it will hold them open. The host asks for one by name, and the provider either grants it, with a lifetime, or refuses it and says why. The registration expires unless it is renewed.

questions: how to register with a hip rendezvous server
how are hip registration lifetimes encoded
subtitle: How a Host Identity Protocol host signs up with a registrar for services such as rendezvous or middlebox traversal.

tldr.problem: A host that uses the Host Identity Protocol may need a service, such as a rendezvous server that helps it find peers, or a middlebox that lets its traffic through. There was no standard way for the host to ask for such a service and for the provider to say yes or no.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds four parameters to the HIP base exchange: REG_INFO, in which a registrar announces which services it offers and for how long, REG_REQUEST, REG_RESPONSE and REG_FAILED. Registration types, lifetimes and failure reasons are encoded in defined fields.
tldr.outcome: A host can register for a service during the HIP base exchange or later over an existing association, and the registration expires on its own unless it is renewed. The RFC obsoletes RFC 5203, which was Experimental.

today: RFC 8003 is a Proposed Standard from October 2016. It obsoletes RFC 5203 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated. The registration parameter types and failure types are registered in the IANA Host Identity Protocol parameters registry.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document specifies an extension to the Host Identity Protocol. The extension provides a generic means for a host to register with a service. The service may, for example, be a HIP rendezvous server or a middlebox.

The document makes no further assumptions about the exact type of service. It also does not specify any mechanisms to discover the presence of specific services or means to interact with them after registration; future documents may describe those operations.
sections.plainLanguage: What is defined here is the sign-up only. How a host finds a service in the first place, and what happens after it has signed up, are left to other documents.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
In addition to the terminology defined in the HIP Architecture, the HIP specification and the HIP Rendezvous Extension, the document defines a requester as a HIP node registering with a HIP registrar to request registration for a service, and a registrar as a HIP node offering registration for one or more services.

A service is a facility that provides requesters with new capabilities or functionalities operating at the HIP layer. Examples include firewalls that support HIP traversal and HIP rendezvous servers.

A registration is shared state stored by a requester and a registrar, allowing the requester to benefit from one or more HIP services offered by the registrar. Each registration has an associated finite lifetime, and requesters can extend established registrations through re-registration, that is, by performing a refresh.

A registration type is an 8-bit identifier for a given service in the registration protocol. For example, the rendezvous service is identified by a specific registration type.
sections.plainLanguage: Three words carry the whole design. A requester wants something, a registrar offers it, and a registration is the standing agreement between them that it has been granted.

sections.title: The Registration Handshake
sections.content:
The document does not specify the means by which a requester discovers the availability of a service or how it locates a registrar. After a requester has discovered a registrar, it either initiates the HIP base exchange or uses an existing HIP association with the registrar. In both cases, registrars use additional parameters to announce their quality and grant or refuse registration, and requesters use corresponding parameters to register with the service.

A host that is capable and willing to act as a registrar should include a REG_INFO parameter in the R1 packets it sends during all base exchanges with that requester. If it is currently unable to provide services because of transient conditions, it should include an empty REG_INFO, one with no services listed. If services can be provided later, it should send UPDATE packets indicating the current set of services available in a new REG_INFO parameter to all hosts it is associated with.

To request registration with a service, a requester constructs and includes a corresponding REG_REQUEST parameter in an I2 or UPDATE packet it sends to the registrar. If the requester has no HIP association established with the registrar, it should send the REG_REQUEST at the earliest possibility, in the I2 packet, which minimizes the number of packets that need to be exchanged. A registrar may end a HIP association that does not carry a REG_REQUEST by including a NOTIFY with the type REG_REQUIRED in the R2, in which case no HIP association is created between the hosts. The REG_REQUIRED notification error type is 51.

Once registration has been requested, the registrar is able to authenticate the requester based on the host identity included in I2. If the registrar knows the Host Identities of all the hosts allowed to register, it should reject registrations from unknown hosts. Since it may be infeasible to preconfigure the registrar with all of them, it should also support HIP certificates to allow for certificate-based authentication.

After successful authorization, the registrar includes a REG_RESPONSE parameter in its response, which contains the service types for which it has authorized registration, and zero or more REG_FAILED parameters containing the service types for which it has not authorized registration or registration has failed for other reasons. This response can be either an R2 or an UPDATE message, depending on whether the registration was requested during the base exchange or using an existing association.

Successful processing of a REG_RESPONSE parameter creates registration state at the requester, and successful processing of a REG_REQUEST parameter creates registration state at the registrar and possibly at the service. Both the requester and the registrar can cancel a registration before it expires, if the services afforded by a registration are no longer needed or can no longer be provided.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways in. During the first handshake, the provider lists what it has and the requester asks for one of them. Or, on a later exchange over a connection that already exists, the same thing happens with UPDATE messages. Either way the provider answers with a grant or with a refusal that names the reason.

sections.title: The Four Parameters
sections.content:
The encoding of the new parameters conforms to the HIPv2 TLV format. REG_INFO has type 930, and its length is in octets excluding the Type, Length and Padding fields. It carries a minimum registration lifetime, a maximum registration lifetime and the registration types offered by the registrar. Registrars include the parameter in R1 packets in order to announce their registration capabilities, and should include it in UPDATE packets when the service offering has changed. The registrar indicates the minimum and maximum registration lifetime that it is willing to offer, and a requester should not request a lifetime greater than the maximum or smaller than the minimum.

REG_REQUEST has type 932. It carries the requested registration lifetime and the preferred registration types in order of preference. A requester includes it in I2 or UPDATE packets. If it is in an UPDATE packet, the registrar must not modify the registrations of registration types that are not listed in the parameter. The requester must not include the parameter unless the registrar's R1 packet or latest received UPDATE packet has contained a REG_INFO parameter with the requested registration types. When the registrar receives a registration with a lifetime that is smaller or greater than the minimum or maximum lifetime, it should grant the registration for the minimum or maximum lifetime respectively.

REG_RESPONSE has type 934. It carries the granted registration lifetime and the granted registration types in order of preference. The registrar should include it only if a registration has successfully completed. The requester must be prepared to receive any registration lifetime, including ones beyond the minimum and maximum lifetime indicated in the REG_INFO parameter, and must not expect that the returned lifetime will be the requested one.

REG_FAILED has type 936. It carries the reason for the failure and the registration types that failed with that reason. The registrar should include it if registration has not completed successfully and the requester is asked to try again with additional credentials.
sections.plainLanguage: Four small pieces of information ride along in the HIP packets: what the provider offers, what the requester wants, what was granted, and what went wrong. Each has its own number in the HIP parameter registry.

sections.title: Encoding Registration Lifetimes
sections.content:
The HIP registration uses an exponential encoding of registration lifetimes. The special value of zero in the lifetime field must be interpreted as representing a lifetime duration of zero seconds, and is used to request and grant cancellation of a registration.

The non-zero values of the lifetime field must be interpreted as an exponent value representing a lifetime duration of 2 to the power of ((lifetime - 64) divided by 8) seconds. This allows a compact encoding of 255 different lifetime durations, in addition to the special lifetime duration of zero seconds, ranging from 2 to the power of (63 divided by 8) seconds, that is about 4 milliseconds, to 2 to the power of (191 divided by 8) seconds, that is about 178 days, into an 8-bit integer field.
sections.plainLanguage: The lifetime is stored as an exponent rather than as a number of seconds, so one byte can cover a range from about four milliseconds to about six months.

sections.title: Establishing and Maintaining Registrations
sections.content:
Establishing or maintaining a registration may require additional information not available in the transmitted REG_REQUEST or REG_RESPONSE parameters, so registration type definitions may define dependencies for HIP parameters that are not defined in this document.

The minimum lifetime both registrars and requesters must support is 10 seconds, while they should support a maximum lifetime of 120 seconds at least. These values define a baseline for the specification of services based on the registration system. They were chosen to be neither too short nor too long, and to accommodate existing timeouts of state established in middleboxes such as NATs and firewalls.

A zero lifetime is reserved for cancelling purposes, and requesting a zero lifetime for a registration type is equal to cancelling the registration of that type. A requester may cancel a registration before it expires by sending a REG_REQUEST to the registrar with a zero lifetime, and a registrar should respond and grant a registration with a zero lifetime. A registrar, and an attached service, may cancel a registration before it expires at its own discretion, but if it does so it should send a REG_RESPONSE with a zero lifetime to all registered requesters.
sections.plainLanguage: The baseline is short on purpose: ten seconds minimum, two minutes desirable. Long registrations would outlive the state a firewall or NAT keeps for a host, so the default is modest and services that need longer can ask for it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extensions described in the document rely on the HIP base exchange and do not modify its security characteristics, such as digital signatures or the Hashed Message Authentication Code. Hence, the only threat introduced by these extensions is related to the creation of soft registration state at the registrar.

Registrars act on a voluntary basis and are willing to accept being a Responder and then to create HIP associations with a number of potentially unknown hosts. Because they have to store HIP association state anyway, adding a certain amount of time-limited HIP registration states should not introduce any serious additional threats, especially because HIP registrars may cancel registrations at any time at their own discretion, for example because of resource constraints during an attack.
sections.plainLanguage: The registration rides inside the signed HIP handshake, so it is as protected as the rest of HIP. The one new thing a registrar has to hold is a bit of extra state per registered host, and that state has a lifetime and can be dropped at any time.

messages.label: I1
messages.note: The requester starts a HIP base exchange.

messages.label: R1 (REG_INFO: S1, S2, S3)
messages.note: The registrar announces the services it offers, with the lifetimes it will accept.

messages.label: I2 (REG_REQUEST: S1)
messages.note: The requester asks to register for service S1.

messages.label: R2 (REG_RESPONSE: S1)
messages.note: The registrar grants the registration for S1.

viz.caption: Registering over an association that already exists, from the RFC's example

messages.label: UPDATE (REG_INFO: S)
messages.note: The registrar announces the services it currently offers.

messages.label: UPDATE (REG_REQUEST: S)
messages.note: The requester asks to register for service S.

viz.caption: The HIP parameter types this RFC defines

items.label: REG_INFO
items.desc: Announces the registration types a registrar offers, with the minimum and maximum registration lifetimes.

items.label: REG_REQUEST
items.desc: Carries the requested registration lifetime and the preferred registration types, in order of preference.

items.label: REG_RESPONSE
items.desc: Carries the granted registration lifetime and the granted registration types.

items.label: REG_FAILED
items.desc: Carries the reason the registration failed and the registration types it applies to.

items.label: Additional credentials required
items.desc: The registrar requires further credentials to authorize the requester.

items.label: Registration type unavailable
items.desc: The requested service type is unavailable at the registrar.

items.label: Insufficient resources
items.desc: The registrar does not currently have enough resources to register the requester.

items.label: Invalid certificate
items.desc: The registrar could not validate the certificate the requester supplied.

items.label: Bad certificate
items.desc: The certificate is corrupt or contains invalid signatures.

items.label: Unsupported certificate
items.desc: The certificate is of an unsupported type.

items.label: Certificate expired
items.desc: The certificate is no longer valid.

items.label: Certificate other
items.desc: The certificate could not be validated for some unspecified reason.

items.label: Unknown CA
items.desc: The issuing certification authority certificate could not be located or is not trusted.

viz.caption: How a registration lifetime is written

items.title: Zero
items.text: A lifetime of zero seconds, used to request or grant the cancellation of a registration.

items.title: Non-zero
items.text: A lifetime of L means a duration of 2 to the power of ((L - 64) divided by 8) seconds.

items.title: Range
items.text: 255 different durations fit in the 8-bit field, from about 4 milliseconds to about 178 days.
